archetype.name: Playoff Team (ball-control)
archetype.definition: A run-leaning, clock-hogging team whose defense wins on early downs and third down. Its efficiency is good enough for January, but it has been dragged around by a three-quarterback carousel and costly giveaways.

report.headline: Better built than last year's 11-win team; the turnovers are what's holding it back
report.take:
This is a team that wants to shorten the game. Chicago leads the league in time of possession at 36.02 minutes a game, passes less than the situation calls for (pass rate over expected of -3.4, 23rd), and leans on a line that gives its backs 2.9 yards before contact. The defense finishes the job by getting off the field: opponents convert just 25.8% of third downs, second-best in the league, and the 8.9% sack rate is also second. Add top-five special teams and you get a team that is 8th in net EPA without a single dominant unit.

The record arrived through a quarterback blender. Caleb Williams started weeks 1, 2 and 6, Case Keenum won both of his starts, and Tyson Bagent's lone start was the 7-31 loss at Green Bay. That game, with five giveaways, explains most of what looks wrong. The season turnover margin is 30th in the league, and the defeat looks like a fluke of an emergency start rather than a trait. Williams came back at Atlanta with 305 passing yards in a win. The other loss was a 3-9 rock fight against Minnesota's top-ranked defense.

Two things in the numbers deserve suspicion. First, the 59-37 opener at Carolina inflates both the scoring and the point differential. Since then the offense has been efficient rather than explosive, 7th in success rate but 14th in EPA. Second, the defense's good pass numbers hide a split personality. It is 3rd in EPA on short passes and dead last in both deep-pass EPA and explosive pass rate allowed. The run defense (25th in EPA) and red-zone defense (22nd) are soft too. Third-down stops and sacks have been covering for all of it.

The history matters here. Last year's 11-6 team was a mirage of luck: 2.82 wins over expected, a league-best turnover margin, and a defense ranked 21st. This version is the reverse, with better underlying play and worse bounces. That is the more sustainable profile. The near-term problem is the pass rush, which loses Montez Sweat to suspension and Dayo Odeyingbo to injured reserve just as the sack rate is propping up the defense.

strengths.title: Getting off the field on third down
strengths.body: Opponents are converting barely a quarter of their third downs. That stat explains why a defense with real holes still ranks 8th in EPA allowed. It is built on a pass rush that wins at a high rate and a secondary that smothers underneath throws. Third-down rates are noisy, though, and this one leans on edge rushers who are now unavailable, so expect it to drift toward average.

strengths.title: Ball control and hidden yardage
strengths.body: The Bears own the clock more than anyone and add field position through special teams that rank 5th in EPA per game. An offense that is 7th in success rate turns into long, grinding drives. That shrinks the game and protects a defense that leaks big plays. This is a scheme identity rather than variance, so it should hold.

strengths.title: Efficient play survived three quarterbacks
strengths.body: A top-10 net EPA with three different starters says the structure travels: a line that is 7th in pressure rate allowed, a 4.33 yards-per-carry run game, and a spread of targets across Luther Burden III, Rome Odunze, Colston Loveland and Kalif Raymond. With Williams back, the ceiling rises. It is also a clear improvement over last season's net EPA, which ranked only 14th.

concerns.title: The deep ball is wide open
concerns.body: No defense allows more EPA on deep passes or a higher explosive pass rate. The underneath coverage is excellent, which suggests the defense is getting beaten over the top rather than everywhere. With the pass rush now thinned, quarterbacks will get more time to find those shots. Against good passing offenses this is the most likely way the Bears lose.

concerns.title: Edge rush gutted for now
concerns.body: Montez Sweat is suspended, with a listed return of November 2, and Dayo Odeyingbo is on injured reserve until late November. Linebacker T.J. Edwards is also out. The sack rate is doing a lot of the defense's heavy lifting, so this hits the unit's engine, not its depth. Expect fewer drive-killing sacks for at least the next two games.

concerns.title: Giveaways and soft run defense
concerns.body: The 11 turnovers are the biggest drag on the record. Most of the damage came in Bagent's five-giveaway start, so with Williams under center this should improve. The run defense is a more structural flaw: it is 25th in EPA allowed and gives up too many explosive runs, and the red-zone defense ranks 22nd. Offenses that can run and finish drives get around the third-down wall.

trend.note: A blowout win, a 3-9 loss, two Keenum wins, a five-turnover collapse at Green Bay and a Williams-led win at Atlanta. The swings track the quarterback more than the team. The Atlanta win came with four sacks allowed and 133 penalty yards, so it was not clean.

nextGame.headline: Depleted Bears pass rush meets Maye's efficient but battered Patriots
nextGame.body:
This is a matchup of styles. New England's offense runs through Drake Maye's arm: 7th in pass EPA and 26th in rush EPA, with the second-longest time to throw in the league. Chicago's defense swallows short passes and gives up the deep ones. The Patriots' defense is ordinary (17th in EPA) and soft against the run (23rd). That sets up the Bears' ground-and-clock approach, and both teams are 30th in turnover margin. The Book has Chicago -3 with a 50.5 total, and both sides come in on a short week.

Availability cuts both ways. Chicago is without Sweat (suspended), Odeyingbo (IR) and Edwards, and lead back insurance Kyle Monangai is out, putting more carries on D'Andre Swift. Guard Jonah Jackson is questionable. New England is in worse shape in key spots. Top corner Carlton Davis III is out along with two depth corners. Three offensive linemen are questionable: Alijah Vera-Tucker, Morgan Moses (seen in a walking boot) and center Ben Brown. A.J. Brown is limited, and Romeo Doubs is on IR.

waysToWin.title: Run at a soft front, own the clock
waysToWin.body: The Patriots rank 23rd in rush EPA allowed. Chicago already leads the league in possession time and leans run. Long Swift-led drives keep Maye on the sideline and lower the number of deep shots he gets at a secondary that leaks them.

waysToWin.title: Attack a corner room without Davis
waysToWin.body: With Carlton Davis III out and two backup corners also out, New England's deep coverage is thinned, and it already ranks 24th in deep EPA allowed. The Patriots have been tough on opposing WR1s and TE1s in PPR terms, so the opening may come through Odunze and Raymond rather than Burden or Loveland.

waysToWin.title: Make Maye hold it behind a patched line
waysToWin.body: Maye holds the ball a long time, and his line already ranks 22nd in pressure rate allowed before its injuries. Even without its two best edge pieces, Chicago's rush can create third-and-long situations where its third-down defense thrives.

waysToLose.title: Maye hits the deep ball
waysToLose.body: A top-10 passing offense against the league's worst deep-pass defense is the obvious danger. That is especially true with the Bears' pass rush missing the players who usually speed up throws. A couple of explosives can erase a long possession advantage in two snaps.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers flip a coin-flip game
waysToLose.body: Both teams sit 30th in turnover margin, so whoever protects the ball likely wins. Chicago's giveaways have been its biggest self-inflicted wound. New England finishes well in the red zone on defense, so any short field the Bears hand over is costly.

waysToLose.title: Protection and penalties stall drives
waysToLose.body: Chicago allowed four sacks in each of its last two games and committed 133 penalty yards at Atlanta. On a short week with Jonah Jackson questionable, drive-killers undo the ball-control plan.

nextGame.watch: Maye's deep attempts against Chicago's safeties. If the Bears' thinned rush can't speed him up, the league's leakiest deep defense is the matchup that decides this game.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying team is sturdier than last year's 11-win group. It has a real defense, a run game that works and special teams that add value. The turnover margin should improve with Williams back, and that is upside the record hasn't banked yet. What should regress is the third-down defense and the sack rate, especially while Sweat and Odeyingbo are out. The opening blowout also flatters the scoring, so expect a lower-scoring team than 25 a game suggests.

The schedule splits. Seattle and Tampa Bay bring top-four defenses right away, and the stretch run is brutal: Buffalo, Green Bay, Detroit twice and Minnesota in the finale. In between, there are friendlier dates with New Orleans, Miami and Jacksonville. Two leaky defenses (Detroit and Buffalo) also face elite offenses that will test Chicago's deep-ball problem. A wild-card berth is the realistic target, with Minnesota's 5-0 start making the division a stretch.
swingFactors: Caleb Williams staying healthy and in the lineup
How the defense holds up until Sweat and Odeyingbo return

confidence.note: Six games split across three quarterbacks, plus one blowout and one five-turnover game skewing the totals, and key edge rushers now out.
